lesson.title: Molecular Scissors: Bacterial Defense Turned Lab Tool
lesson.summary: Restriction enzymes are proteins that cut DNA at specific short recognition sequences, an evolutionary defense bacteria use against invading viruses, now used by scientists as precise molecular scissors.
lesson.body:
Restriction enzymes did not evolve for scientists' convenience, they evolved as a bacterial immune defense. Bacteria are under constant attack from bacteriophages, viruses that inject their own DNA into the bacterial cell. To fight back, many bacteria produce restriction enzymes that chop up any DNA carrying a specific target sequence. The obvious problem is that the bacterium's own genome also contains that sequence somewhere, so bacteria protect themselves by methylating, adding a methyl group to, their own DNA at those exact sites, the same kind of chemical tag covered in DNA methylation, which prevents the bacterium's own restriction enzyme from cutting its own genome while still destroying unmethylated viral DNA. This pairing of a cutting enzyme with a protective methylation system is called a restriction-modification system, and it is a striking real-world example of the substrate specificity that defines how enzymes work in general.

Each restriction enzyme recognizes one specific short DNA sequence, typically four to eight base pairs long, and that sequence is usually palindromic, meaning it reads the same 5' to 3' on both strands. A classic, well-studied example is EcoRI, isolated from E. coli, which recognizes the sequence GAATTC and cuts the sugar-phosphate backbone between the G and the A on each strand:

5'-G     A A T T C-3'
3'-C T T A A     G-5'

Because the two cuts are offset rather than directly across from each other, this leaves short single-stranded overhangs, in this case AATT, called sticky ends. Any other DNA fragment cut by EcoRI, regardless of what organism it came from, will end up with the exact same complementary overhang, and because DNA follows the same base pairing rules everywhere, those sticky ends can pair up with each other.

That compatibility is the whole reason restriction enzymes became central to biotechnology: sticky ends generated by the same enzyme, even from completely different sources, will spontaneously find and base pair with one another, which is exactly the trick used to combine DNA from different sources in DNA cloning and recombinant DNA technology, covered in later sections. Not every restriction enzyme leaves an overhang, some cut straight across both strands at the same position, producing what is called a blunt end instead, but the sticky-end cutters are the ones most often used to build recombinant DNA constructs. Restriction enzymes are, in effect, the first tool reached for in the biotechnology toolkit introduced earlier, the precise scissors that make everything downstream possible.
